html:
Taputapuātea, on the island of Raiatea, was the greatest marae, or stone ceremonial site, of East Polynesia. From around 1000 CE it was the centre of worship of the god ʻOro.

Priests and chiefs from many islands came to Raiatea, and a stone from Taputapuātea was taken to found new marae elsewhere. Raiatea was remembered as Havaiki, the homeland, in the traditions of the voyagers who settled Hawaii, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa.

The navigator Tupaia, who sailed with Cook, trained here. The site lost its role after Christianity spread through the islands following the missionaries, and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017.
sum: Taputapuātea, on the island of Raiatea, was the greatest marae, or stone ceremonial site, of East Polynesia. From around 1000 CE it was the centre of worship of the god ʻOro.
